course.title: Overseer Geology Refresher Training
course.description: Geology refresher training for production overseers

modules.title: Mining Geology
modules.description: An introduction to geology relevant to mining

steps.title: Geology Introduction
steps.html:
• Geology is the study of the earth and rock forming processes
  • Rocks are made of different minerals depending on where and how they are formed 
  • Sedimentary rocks are formed by mineral particles being deposited and pressed into layers (strata)
  • Examples of sedimentary rocks are sandstone, mudstone and limestone

Mining Relevance
  • Some minerals are valuable or have special properties (Polyhalite), others are waste, reduce the grade or can cause problems (Salt)
  • The minerals that the rocks are made of, and how they are cemented together determines the rocks strength
  • Rock strength determines how easy the rock is to mine and how strong and stable the mining roof and sidewalls are

images.caption: Rivers and beaches create sandstone
lakes and deep seas create mudstones
Tropical reefs and warm seas create limestone

steps.title: Evaporites
steps.html:
• Salt, Polyhalite and Potash are Sedimentary rocks called Evaporites.
  • Evaporites form in hot and dry climates where sea water is evaporated and salts crystalise
  • 75m of seawater must be evaporated to create 1m of Rock Salt (Halite)

Mining Relevance
  • Evaporites are made of crystals. Larger crystals are harder to cement together which makes the rock weaker
  • Evaporites can form in layers, which can act as planes of weakness and failure

images.caption: Salt crystals accumulating from the evaporating sea water

steps.title: Geological Structures
steps.html:
• Rocks can also have structures which can effect their strength and behaviour when mined
  • Faults  can reduce rock strength and allow oils or gases to enter the mine through fractures.
  • Faults can also offset the seam creating steep dips
  • Layers of rock are called Beds or Bedding Planes. Each layer/bed is discontinuity (break)  which can act as a plane of weakness or failure.
  • When rocks are compressed, they can buckle and Fold

2 Faults which have displaced the black layers

steps.title: Boulby Mine Structures
steps.html:
• Boulby Mine has examples of both Faulting and Folding
  • Potash was commonly folded creating thicker and thinner seams with high dips
  • There are major faults in the mine which have caused us to have to mine up significant gradients (North 1 Fault in Salt) or released oil into the roads (2000 Salt)

modules.title: Polyhalite Geology
modules.description: The geology of the polyhalite seam and the hazards that can be present

steps.title: Overview
steps.html:
There are 2 operating levels of the mine currently - Polyhalite and Salt. 


The diagram below shows the position of the different rock units at the mine and the mine infrastructure.
It also shows the potential major hazards associated with the geology of these areas.

images.caption: Section showing the different mining levels, rock layers and associated hazards
The different mining levels and associated hazards

steps.title: Polyhalite Overview
steps.html:
• The current mining area for Polyhalite is called Discovery also referred to as  (Zone 1). Below is the generalised structure of the geology of Zone 1. 
  • The polyhalite seam is around 15m thick but varies across Zone 1.  
  • The Polyhalite seam has been characterised into 3 layers termed P1, P2 and P3, with P1 at the top and P3 at the bottom
  • The rock immediately above Polyhalite is Salt
  • the rocks below Polyhalite are Anhydrite then Dolomite

images.caption: Schematic cross-section through the Zone 1 Polyhalite Geology
The Polyhalite Mining Level

steps.title: Polyhalite P3
steps.html:
• The lower P3 Polyhalite is the highest grade. The target mining horizon is typically 3-5m above the base of seam
  • Polyhalite is finely layered with darker and lighter bands
  • P2 has more salt bands which get thicker the higher up you go, until the ultimate roof of the polyhalite is Salt.
  • P1 is around 1m thick and is not relevant to mining.
Hazards
  • The layers in polyhalite can delaminate when vertical stress is reduced or shear when horizontal stress increases
  • Polyhalite contains H2S gas within its crystals. When the rock is broken this gas is released
  • The more rock that is broken simultaneously, the more gas is released.
  • Other minerals such as Glauberite have more space between crystals allowing them to hold more volumes of H2S

images.caption: High grade P3 Polyhalite

steps.title: Polyhalite P2
steps.html:
• P2 Polyhalite is above the P3 and has more salt bands with increasing thickness
  • Mining higher in the seam increases the amount of halite (salt) that is present which reduces the quality of the ore 
Hazards
  • Salt is weaker than Polyhalite so  reduces the strength of the roof beam and pillars
  • The salt bands often have a clay/shale margin above and below the salt. This can form a plane of weakness which can result in delamination, shear and roof issues (ripping).

images.caption: P2 Polyhalite with intermixed salt
P2 Polyhalite with multiple salt bands
Delamination on shale parting during mining.
smooth and humpy surface of shale parting

steps.title: Polyhalite Base of Seam
steps.html:
• The base of the Polyhalite seam is the 'Footwall' Anhydrite
  • Anhydrite is stronger and harder to mine than Polyhalite and will reduce the quality of the ore
  • The base of seam is variable and can step up or down sharply

Hazards
  • Beneath the Anhydrite is a rock called the Kirkham Abbey Dolomite
  • In local areas of the mine, this Dolomite is fractured and can store Methane Gas. 
  • Mining closer to the base of seam may increase the likelihood of this gas being released 

Other factors also influence gas release:
  1. Whether there are fractures present and if these fractures contain gas
  2. Whether the mining intersects these fractures by mining or drilling into them
  3. The extent of mining induced fracturing in the floor. Retreat mining, particularly stubs which increase the span (width), reduces the vertical stress in the floor allowing it to relax and fracture
  4. The presence of geological structures such as faults

images.caption: Base of seam 'Footwall Ahydrite' contact with the P3 Polyhalite
The contact between polyhalite (smooth) and anhydrite (very small crystals)
Section view showing the base of seam stepping up 4m infront of the mining
Mechanism for Methane Gas release in Polyhalite

modules.title: Salt Geology
modules.description: The geology of the Boulby Salt and the hazards that can be present

steps.title: Overview
steps.html:
• Salt mining takes place in the Boulby Halites (Salt). There are 9 different layers of boulby halite
  • Immediately above the salt is the Boulby Potash, then Marl and eventually the Bunter Sandstone
  • The potash and marl can present a ground control (weaker) and gas risk
  • The Bunter Sandstone can present a water inrush risk if significant faults are present, or through over mining creating fractures.
  • Below the Boulby Salts is the Billingham Main Anhydrite which can present a gas risk

images.caption: The position of the Boulby Salt Mining Level relative to surrounding rocks.
Weaker marl roof fall in unbolted mining pass.
Methane and nitrogen gas blow in potash
inflow of water from the Bunter Sandstone from mining induced fracturing

steps.title: Polygons
steps.html:
• Salt mining tries to stay around 10m below the base of the Boulby Potash
  • Salt mining must stop if it gets within 2m of the Potash due to the roof becoming weak and requiring additional supports

  • The target mining horizon for Salt  is the BH5 called Polygons 
  • The Polygons are located around 10-15m below the Boulby Potash
  • The Polygons are the cleanest and highest grade salt and are geotechnically stable compared to other salts 
  • Large crystals and increased shale/clay content makes the salt weaker

  • Mining higher in the Boulby Halites increases the amount of potash enrichment in the Salts
  • Mining lower in the Boulby Halites increases the amount of anhydrite and shale content in the Salt reducing its quality

modules.title: Exploration Drilling
modules.description: The purpose and hazards of exploration drilling and their relationship with mining operations

steps.title: Exploration Drilling 1
steps.html:
The purpose of exploration drilling is to identify potential hazards and to find new areas to mine. 

Exploration drilling produces drill core which is examined, documented and sampled by geologists. Exploration drilling provides information including:

  • Geology and seam characteristics 
  • Seam Thickness 
  • Seam Grade and Quality 
  • Base and Top of Seam Elevations 
  • Seam Gradient 
  • Geological Hazards (Faults, gas, hydrocarbons) 
  • Areas of thin seam or no seam 

This information is used for mine planning and safety

images.caption: An exploration or 'long hole' drill rig

steps.title: Exploration Drilling 2
steps.html:
• Exploration drilling can be sub-horizonal or sub-vertical. 
  • Horizonal drilling can explore laterally in front by distances of up to 3 km whereas vertical drilling is typically around 150-200m.
  • Exploration boreholes are shown on mine plans as coloured lines. The hole name is shown as text at the end of hole position.
  • Blue lines are Polyhalite holes, Brown lines are Potash holes.

images.caption: Blue lines representing the location of polyhalite boreholes
Brown lines representing the location of potash boreholes

steps.title: Exploration Drilling 3
steps.html:
A drill bay is made up of 3 components:

  • The widened / fanned out drilling bay 
  • The Sump 
  • The Core stub      


Drill bays are designed to facilitate productive drilling and it is vital that they are mined to plan.

Drilling uses a concentrated brine to lubricate the bit and return the core. The main drill bay floor is mined upwards to allow drilling brine to flow down into the milled out sump where it can be pumped back into the drill hole.


  • Never add or dispose of nuisance water into an active drill-bay sump without approval from the drilling manager. 
  • Adding fresh water to the brine can dilute it and result in leaching of the hole walls. 
  • If the hole is leached at the face this can compromise the seal forcing the hole to be abandoned potentially losing months of work.

images.caption: standard layout for an exploration drill bay

steps.title: Drilling Hazards 1
steps.html:
Exploration drilling involves breaking of ground into unknown areas or areas suspected to be hazardous. These areas can host hazards such as brines, gases and oils.

The major hazards  associated with drilling are inrush and outburst


These hazards are mitigated by:

  • Avoiding drilling potentially hazardous areas if possible 
  • Drilling through a standpipe which is sealed into the face with specialist cemented and pressure tested to 2000psi 
  • Drilling through a blow-out preventer (BOP) to prevent rod string and brine from being ejected from the hole under pressure 
  • Having a shear-ram which can be operated in the event of an emergency to cut the rod string and seal the hole. 
  • Equipment is linked to methane detector and automatic cut-out. 
  • Having adequate ventilation to dilute gas occurrences 
  • Preferably siting drill bays in return roadways 
  • Using handheld XRF to identify the base of polyhalite seam and minimise drilling into the base of seam 
  • A methane drainage line which can be used to drain methane to outbye areas (top of drift).

images.caption: Shear ram in position on drill hole collar
Shear ram is operated from the accumulated located in fresh air at the bay entrance
Drill bay gas line which can be used to drain gas from a borehole into the returns

steps.title: Drilling Hazards 2
steps.html:
• Each drill bay is equipped with a methane drainage line. This is a sealed network of pipes which runs outbye to the top of the drift in poly, or outbye of 17XC on 2000 Salt. In the event of methane inflow, the gas line can be connected to the back of the drill rods and the gas drained out.
  • The gas is drained outbye to the top of the drift where it is put back into the general body of air. At the top of the drift the volume of air is substantially larger than the returns of the drill bay giving it greater ability to dilute the methane down to safe levels.
  • Never damage or interfere with the gas line without approval. If you discover a defect to the gas line such as damage or split pipes report it immediately to the drill bay and CRO.
  • A number of exploration boreholes have encountered methane gas, one of which - P003 was under significant pressure and volumes.
  • Holes which encounter methane may still remain a hazard even after plugging or drainage.
  • Holes which have encountered gas will be shown on the mining plan as a green precautionary zone. Additional control measures may be required to mine in these areas.
  • Boreholes which are intersected in the mining faces should be recorded on the Stat Report and reported to the Geology department

images.caption: plan showing a borehole which is a precautionary zone (green)

steps.title: Exploration Drilling & Mining
steps.html:
It is important to know the location of active drill bays in relation to the panel or area you are in charge of.

Things to consider include:

•Is the drill bay part of your inspection?

•How does the drill bay ventilation system relate to your ventilation circuit?

•How many people are in a drill bay and how often are they working in there?

•Do you require OxyK self rescuers to enter and where are they located?

•If methane was encountered while mining, how would this impact the drill bay and vice versa? • •Where is drill bay and drill bay fans powered from?

•Do you share the same egress to a safe haven?

•Where is the methane drainage line located and what is it’s condition?

steps.title: Exploration Drilling Outputs
steps.html:
• Exploration Drilling information allows us to estimate the grade and tonnes in the ground (Mineral Resources) and design future mining areas (Ore Reserves)
  • It also identifies areas to avoid with the mining due to low grade, steep seam dip or hazards.

modules.title: Geological Data - Plans and Sections
modules.description: Understanding mining plans and geology sections

steps.title: Geological Assessment & Authorised Mining Plans
steps.html:
• Before an area can be mined, an Authorised Plan must be issued
  • A plan can only be authorised when each technical department has considered the design and any potential risks
  • A geological assessment is completed to consider the available geological information with respect to safety, quality(grade) and mining(gradient) risks.
  • If an area is deemed to be of increased risk of inrush, this is called a precautionary zone  and is shown as a green outline
  • To mine within a precautionary zone, a managers scheme of work must be in place with additional control measures to mitigate the increased risk.

images.caption: Example geological assessment matrix

steps.title: Authorised Plans
steps.html:
• An authorised plan contains the signatures of the relevant responsible persons
  • Only the authorised plan can be used for mining operations
  • The authorised plan cannot be altered by hand using pen or pencil. Any changes to the plan must be undertaken digitally by the survey department.
  • This is because no single person at the mine holds all the information around conditions and risk. Any change must be re-considered by all relevant departments.

images.caption: An example of an Authorised plan with signature box
Example of prohibited hand drawn alteration to an authorised plan

steps.title: Geological Sections
steps.html:
Geology sections are available for all roads in the mine
Sections are updated by recording:
  •  the changes in height of the datum line
  • the distance of the roof above the datum line
  • the total floor-roof height
  • The position, angle and readings of probe hole drilling
  • Base of seam estimate interpreted from the probing results

In the example image, the following features are numbered:
  1. Roof and floor position (thick black lines)
  2. Existing downhole with probe readings
  3. existing s/c hole with readings
  4. interpreted base of seam / anhydrite position from probe readings
  5. planned future mining
  6. planned future drilling
  7. Estimated intersection position of Exploration (LHD) boreholes.
  8. Estimated geological surfaces derived from exploration boreholes. purple = top of P3 Polyhalite, green/blue = base of seam.

modules.title: Geology & Rock Mechanics
modules.description: An overview of the relationship between Geology and Rock Mechanics

steps.title: Rock Stress - 1
steps.html:
• Stress is the term which describes the forces acting upon a rock.
  • Stress can be in 3 forms – tension, compression and shear
  • Tensile stress is when material is being pulled apart under extension. Rocks are weakest when under tension.
  • Compression stress is when a rock is squished. Rocks are strong under compression up to a failure point.
  • Shear stress is when rocks slide past each other. When forces act upon surfaces at low angles or when compressional forces or rock strengths are un-even, shear can occur.

steps.title: Rock Stress - 2
steps.html:
• Rock stress occurs in 3 dimensions. 
  • Forces can result due to the weight of overlying rock – overburden and tectonic / regional stress.
  • Boulby is a deep, high stress environment. 
  • The main force is compressional and vertical due to overlying rocks. 
  • The horizontal stresses are mainly a result of confinement. The forces are broadly equal with vertical being slightly greater.

steps.title: Rock Stress - 3
steps.html:
• Stress concentrates in the pillars and in the roof-pillar corners.
  • The roof beam is destressed in the vertical sense as the weight sits on the pillars. This allows the roof to relax 
  • geological layers in the roof can open and become detached as discontinuities, or sheared by horizontal stress.

images.caption: Model representations of how vertical stress is redistributed around the mining heading and concentrated in the pillars
Pillar taking vertical load. Fractures open perpendicular to stress direction. 'Apple coring' starting to show
Roof /lip is vertically de-stressed, horizontal stress is increased, promoting fractures to open perpendicular to the horizontal stress.

steps.title: Rock Strain - 1
steps.html:
• When rocks are put under stress they can begin to deform. This deformation is called strain
  • Elastic deformation returns to their original shape when the force is removed – think about stretching and then releasing an elastic band - it returns to its original shape when the force is removed
  • Plastic deformation are deformed irreversibly, when the stress is removed they remain in the deformed shape – think about squeezing plasticine.

Rock Engineers conduct tests on samples to see how they respond to increasing stress.

Lets look at how a Polyhalite pillar might behave as stress is progressively increased:

steps.title: Rock Strain - 2
steps.html:
• The mineral composition of a rock controls its strength. 
  • Rocks made of strong minerals and with no structures or weaknesses in them can tolerate a lot of stress.
  • Uniform, strong rocks may not show any signs of stress loading, spalling or failure.
  • Once the stress exceeds the rocks strength the pillar can fail suddenly and catastrophically called a rock burst
  • This is why the RED department install stress cells. This lets them monitor the stress conditions of pillars which might not show any signs of loading or failure

steps.title: Plastic Deformation
steps.html:
• Different rocks respond and deform differently based on their properties
  • Potash and Salt can progressively deform by squeezing and creep
  • Think about tell tale movements, chocks and roadway closure

images.caption: Roof lowering and closure in salt
Historical roadway closure

steps.title: Brittle Deformation
steps.html:
• Different rocks respond and deform differently based on their properties

  • A Polyhalite is more brittle and tends to deform elastically. 

  • Polyhalite can take load before failing suddenly. This is why correct pillar design, survey control and mining to plan is important

images.caption: Polyhalite pillar failure due to small pillar size

steps.title: Geology & Rock Strength
steps.html:
• Rock failure is a result of the stress forces exceeding the rock strength.
  • For a rock to fail the stress can be increased beyond the strength or the rock strength can be reduced below the typical stress.


Geological features determine the rock strength:

•The mineral composition – some minerals are stronger than others due to crystal shape and structure.

•crystal/grain size – larger grains can be harder to hold together and more easily fractured

•cohesion, compaction and cementation of grains of mineral

•homogeneity vs heterogeneity – mixtures of minerals and features are generally weaker.

•Geological structures including fractures, faults and bedding planes – shape, and infill
